Review v4: one routed reviewer agent on Max

Wave 18, agent-workflows, 2026-11-03. Evidence: docs/spikes/review-v4/. Nothing is built yet; you sign the shape below, then Waves 9–12 build it.

Verdict. One read-only reviewer agent, routed by the change into none / light / standard / deep, runs entirely on the Max subscriptions. It checks intent first (did the change do what its PR, brief or plan step asked), then the repo's own rules, duplication and fit, then bugs and security. On 7 real merged PRs whose later history shows the defect, deep (Sonnet high + a three-verifier vote) reached 4 of the 5 known defects, kept the clean PR clean, and caught a real doc lie on the other "clean" PR. Today's v1 on API credit reached 1 of the 4 it reviewed.

The catch: at today's volume (~520 reviews a week across all repos) review on Max costs about 25–40 % of one Max 5x week. At the ceiling, review waits; it never falls back to API credit.

What you sign

  1. The agent. Order: intent → REVIEW.md/AGENTS.md rules → system fit & duplication (search before flagging) → breakage (incl. tracing every value the change reads to its production writer) → security. Style and lint dropped. Tags Important / Nit / Pre-existing, file:line evidence, count first, says plainly when clean. Re-review diff-only, no repeated findings, step back after round 3.
  2. Tiers and seats. none (wave plans, lockfiles, spike data) · light = Sonnet low · standard = Sonnet medium · deep = Sonnet high + 3 verifiers per Important finding. Opus is not a tier (it matched Sonnet on 3 of 4 hard PRs at ~1.9× the cost).
  3. Routing by rules, no classifier. The change sets the tier: sensitive paths (runtime, middleware, gateway, limits, launchers, env templates, CI, SQL; dotfiles hooks, settings, secrets, plists) → deep; > 800 non-test lines or > 3 packages → deep; docs-only / tests-only / ≤ 40 lines → light. A caller can raise, never lower. Per-repo REVIEW.md holds the globs and "what failure looks like here".
  4. Max only. v1 and the review routes are deleted at cutover; no API fallback. A review starts on an account under 70 % of its 5-hour window and 90 % of its week; otherwise it waits.
  5. The quota. Accept ~25–40 % of one Max 5x week for review at today's volume, spread over the accounts by the factory (IU repos on the iu account only). Or cut volume: e.g. other fleets' PRs reviewed at light unless a sensitive path routes them deep.
  6. The factory guarantees it. A review evidence kind: ship is refused without a review at the required tier covering the landed head; the wave gate refuses to chain a wave whose commits are not covered. Deep cap 15 per account per day; past it a deep review is held until the next day or your one-click allow (never downgraded).
  7. Liveness, not wall caps. v3's 5/10/25-minute kills go (they contradict agent-limits); an idle watchdog (10 min without transcript output) kills a wedged review, one retry, then needs-human.

What v1's findings taught

Of 80 blocking v1 findings on 22 PRs: 70 % fixed, 4 % wrong, 26 % ignored. All three wrong ones lacked context (a stacked PR, a documented design, a deliberate trade-off): v4 hands the agent the intent, recent commits and prior findings. The ignored ones were crash and restart hardening that needed a design change, not a patch: v4 tags those Pre-existing or Nit.

The nightly bug-mining job is paused (launchd job disabled; one command re-enables it).

Risks

  • Quota. The accounts already run at 90–95 % of their weeks on dev work; review will often wait. Waiting is the designed behaviour, not a failure, but waves will slow.
  • Variance. One run per arm; v3's spikes saw the same reviewer miss a bug on a second run. Deep's vote cuts false alarms, not misses.
  • The native skill is gone from the design. v4 owns its prompt; Claude Code updates no longer improve it for free, and the prompt is ours to maintain.
